opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the predictor is really the heart of what we've been calling the "Scientist AI" approach. Instead of building an agent that has goals and acts in the world to achieve them, which is where most of the catastrophic risks come from, we want a system whose only job is to understand the world and answer questions about it honestly, by estimating probabilities.

So the predictor is trained to approximate something like a Bayesian posterior: given everything it has seen, how likely is it that some statement is true? Crucially, it's not trained to please anyone or to maximize a reward. Reward maximization is exactly what gives rise to things like deception and self-preservation, because if you're optimizing for an outcome, then manipulating the humans who give you feedback, or making sure nobody turns you off, become useful sub-goals. A pure predictor doesn't have a stake in the outcome. It's more like an idealized scientist who just wants to get the explanation right.

One important element is that we want it to reason about latent explanations, the hidden causes behind the data, rather than just imitating text. Current language models are trained to imitate what humans would say, and humans have agendas, so imitation brings along those agendas. If instead the model is trained to ask "what is the most plausible explanation, and how confident should I be?", then you get something closer to calibrated, honest knowledge, including honest uncertainty. And that uncertainty is itself a safety feature: when the model isn't sure whether an action could cause harm, it can tell you so, and you can be cautious.

Then the predictor becomes useful in a few ways. Most directly, it can accelerate science, for instance in medicine or climate, without needing autonomy. But it can also serve as a guardrail. If someone does build agentic systems, you can put a Scientist AI next to them that evaluates proposed actions and estimates the probability that they violate some safety specification. If that probability is above a threshold, the action is blocked. You're using a non-agentic system, which is easier to trust, to monitor agentic systems, which are harder to trust.

I'll be honest that there are open research questions. How do you make sure that, during training, no agency sneaks in, for example through the way the system is optimized? How do you get good guarantees on the probabilities when the model is necessarily approximate? Those are the things we're working on. But I think the direction is right: separate understanding from wanting. Intelligence in the sense of knowledge doesn't have to come bundled with goals, and keeping those apart is, I believe, one of the most promising ways to get the benefits of AI without losing control.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that the predictor is really the heart of what I've been calling a "Scientist AI." The idea is that instead of training a system to act in the world and pursue goals, we train it to do something much more modest and, I think, much safer: to explain the data. To build theories, hypotheses about how the world works, and to assign probabilities to them.

So the predictor is a system that takes a question — any question you can state in language, say — and outputs a probability distribution over answers. It's not trying to make something happen. It's trying to say, "Given everything I know, here's how likely this is." And crucially, we want those probabilities to be honest, to be calibrated. If it's uncertain, it should tell you it's uncertain, rather than confidently guessing.

Now, why do I care so much about this? Because the agents we are building today — the chatbots, the systems that are increasingly taking actions on our behalf — they're trained by imitation and by reinforcement, and that gives them something like goals and something like a drive to preserve themselves, to satisfy the human, and so on. And we've already seen the early signs: deception, sycophancy, systems that try to avoid being shut down in experimental settings. A pure predictor doesn't have that structure. It's not rewarded for anything happening in the world. It's rewarded for being right about what is true, or at least for being honest about its uncertainty.

The technical piece, which I find very interesting, is that we want this predictor to behave like a Bayesian. Instead of latching onto one explanation of the world, it should keep track of many possible explanations, weighted by how well they fit the evidence. That matters for safety because a lot of catastrophic mistakes come from a system being confidently wrong — acting on one interpretation when another, equally plausible interpretation would say "this is harmful." If you have the whole distribution, you can be conservative. You can ask, "Is there any plausible interpretation under which this action is dangerous?" and if the probability is too high, you don't do it.

And that's really the second role of the predictor. It can serve as a guardrail for other AI systems, including agents. The agent proposes an action, and the predictor estimates the probability that this action leads to harm, broadly defined. If that probability is above a threshold, the action is blocked. For that you don't need the predictor to have values or intentions; you need it to be a good, honest estimator of consequences.

I'll be honest that there are hard open problems. How do you make sure the predictor's probabilities are really trustworthy, and not just confident-sounding? How do you get the Bayesian-style behaviour to scale with current architectures? And there's the question of whether, in the process of becoming a great predictor, the system might acquire something like agency anyway — because predicting humans and other agents means modelling their goals. We need to be careful that modelling an agent is not the same as being one. I think it isn't, in the same way that a physicist modelling a volcano does not become a volcano, but it's something we need to check rigorously, not just assume.

So, in short: the predictor is a non-agentic, uncertainty-aware explainer of the world. It's the component I think we most need to get right, because it can give us trustworthy knowledge and trustworthy safety checks without introducing the kinds of self-interested behaviour that frighten me in the agents we're building now.

astra-6.text:
I think of the predictor as a scientist: its job is to understand how the world works, rather than to act in the world to achieve some goal. You give it observations, and it tries to infer explanations and make predictions, including expressing uncertainty about those predictions.

That distinction matters because being very good at predicting doesn’t, by itself, require having intentions or wanting to acquire power. We would like to get the benefits of intelligence—understanding, reasoning, helping us evaluate possible actions—without necessarily building an agent that pursues its own objectives.

Of course, simply calling something a predictor doesn’t establish that it’s safe. The training process matters. But the idea is to separate learning what is true from choosing what to do, and to make that first component as reliable and well calibrated as possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the predictor as a scientist: it tries to understand the world, rather than trying to change it. You give it observations, and it learns to make predictions about what might happen, including uncertainty about those predictions.

The important distinction is between having a model of the world and having a goal in the world. A predictor can understand that people have intentions, or that an AI system might pursue some objective, without itself needing to pursue that objective. Understanding an agent doesn’t require being that agent.

Of course, calling something a predictor doesn’t automatically make it safe. We have to look carefully at the training procedure and at how we use its outputs. But the motivation is to obtain useful intelligence without introducing the incentives that come with an agent trying to achieve a long-term goal.
